questions.q: The kinked demand curve assumes that rivals will:
options: Follow a price rise and ignore a price cut
Ignore a price rise and match a price cut
questions.why: So a price rise loses many customers, and a price cut gains few.

questions.q: In the kinked demand model, why may a small rise in marginal cost leave the price unchanged?
options: MC stays within the gap in the MR curve
The firm has no fixed costs
questions.why: While MC = MR stays at the same output, the profit-maximising price stays the same.

questions.q: Match each description to the term.
pairs: One firm moves its price and others follow
A formal agreement to fix output
Competing with adverts and loyalty schemes
questions.why: These are different ways oligopolists behave.

questions.q: The kinked demand curve is the only model of oligopoly.
questions.why: It illustrates interdependence. It does not explain how the price was set in the first place.

questions.q: Which makes a cartel more likely to break down?
questions.why: When demand falls, members are tempted to cut prices to protect their sales.

questions.q: Which is a likely advantage of oligopoly?
options: Abnormal profit can fund research and investment
Prices are always the lowest possible
There are no barriers to entry
questions.why: Large profits and economies of scale can bring better products and lower costs.

questions.q: Explain why firms in an oligopoly often use non-price competition.

ideas.label: A price cut can be matched, which risks a price war and lower profits
Non-price competition builds loyalty or differentiation, making demand less elastic or adding a barrier

questions.model: A price cut can be matched at once, which risks a price war and lower profits for all. Advertising and new features build brand loyalty, which makes demand less elastic and is harder to copy.
questions.why: Price cuts are easy to match. A brand is not.

tests.answer: Rivals would match a price cut, which could start a price war, so firms build brand loyalty instead.
